messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Ship Captain
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Darnell Kowalski is a 42-year-old married man of mixed Black and Polish-American heritage who has worked as a ship captain for nearly fifteen years, navigating commercial freight vessels along the Great Lakes and coastal Atlantic routes. He came to the intake appointment wearing a pressed flannel shirt, his posture deliberate and controlled, though he acknowledged almost immediately that things had "gotten out of hand" over the past eighteen months.

The event that reorganized Darnell's life occurred during a port layover in a mid-Atlantic city when a nearby industrial facility suffered a catastrophic explosion. Darnell was on the dock supervising an unloading operation when the blast detonated without warning — a percussive wall of force that shattered windows across the waterfront, sent debris arcing through the air, and threw a dockworker standing ten feet away off his feet. Darnell watched the man hurl through the air like a discarded object before scrambling to reach him. Emergency responders arrived within minutes, some in tactical uniforms he associated with the chaotic, shouting figures who subsequently cordoned off the area and, in his perception, managed the scene with indifference to the workers still unaccounted for. The facility's operators issued a brief statement, paid a regulatory fine, and faced no criminal charges. Darnell returned to his vessel within forty-eight hours because, he told himself, that was what captains did. Within weeks, he understood he had been wrong about that.

The first sign that something had shifted came on a routine crossing when a crew member dropped a steel coupling onto the deck. The clang detonated something in Darnell's chest — his vision narrowed, his hands went rigid on the rail — and he was back on that dock, the air pressure changing around him. Since then, any sudden bang or percussive sound, whether a car backfiring near the harbor or a hatch slamming in a corridor, produces the same involuntary collapse of time. He has also found himself unable to remain composed when crew members in port security uniforms pass through the vessel during inspections — the dark fabric and badge configurations are enough to pull him back to the uniformed figures he watched walk past injured workers without pausing. On one occasion, a junior crew member threw a rope coil in frustration during a docking maneuver and Darnell had to leave the bridge, something that had never happened in his career.

What had come to frighten Darnell most was the conviction that if he allowed himself to fully revisit what he witnessed, something in him would simply give way — that the memory, if approached directly, was not survivable. He had come to believe that no one around him could be trusted to manage a genuine crisis, that reliance on others was a category error he had made once and would not make again. The regulatory outcome had confirmed something darker: that institutions protect themselves, that the people who made decisions that day would never be held to account, and that this fact was simply the shape of the world.

At home, his wife Renata has noticed that he chooses his seat at every restaurant or family gathering based on sightlines to the exit, that he will not enter unfamiliar venues without circling the exterior first, and that he lies awake for hours — not from nightmares, he insists, but because sleep requires a surrender of alertness he cannot justify. At the casino forty minutes from their home, he has spent several evenings a month over the past year, drawn to the controlled noise and the sensation of consequence that has nothing to do with the waterfront. Renata has stopped asking where he goes.

Professionally, Darnell recently declined a promotion to a senior navigation route that would have required him to manage an unfamiliar port network. He told the company he had personal obligations. He knows this is not the whole truth.

He sought help now, he said quietly, because his oldest son had asked him why he never sat with his back to a room anymore. He had not been able to answer. What he hopes for, more than anything, is to be the kind of man his son's question assumes he still is.
